title: "Mentoring Philosophy"
subtitle: "How we work together in this lab"
---

[Mentoring]{.eyebrow}

::: {.lead}
I want most of all to help my students learn how to think about complex problems
in biology, and how to apply their analytical skills to the larger issues they
will face as citizens.
:::

My goal in mentoring at all levels is to give students the tools they need to
apply new knowledge to other advanced subjects. **I want my students to gain the
ability to think critically and to use the scientific method to analyze problems
and draw logical conclusions.**

Through achieving this goal, I hope my mentees develop independence. That
requires teaching students how to break down a problem, how to critically
analyze data, and how to reach an answer supported by evidence. When students
acquire analytical skills to solve problems, they gain the ability to apply what
they have learned to new problems and come up with creative solutions.

Both of my parents were high school teachers, and they showed me that I must
take an active role helping students understand the challenge of a new subject.
Success requires assessing student comprehension and revising my methods in
light of what proves effective. I strive to be responsive to the individual
needs of my mentees.

Teaching at all levels should provide not only content about the particular
subject, but also opportunities to learn about the process of doing science.
Giving students the story of how data are collected or experiments are designed
gives them a clearer understanding of the scientific method. **Teaching students
about the process of science develops their analytical toolbox so they can apply
their knowledge to new areas.** Perhaps the best way to learn the scientific
method is to have the opportunity to do research.

During my graduate and postdoctoral career, I mentored several undergraduate and
graduate students on research projects. In one long-term survey of genetic
diversity, the student and I discussed the sampling design before collecting any
data, and she chose a portion to work on. We read background material on the
molecular techniques and then applied them by sequencing DNA from field
collected snails. Because her research was part of a larger survey, she could
put her work into a more complete context. At the end of the project she
presented her research as an honors thesis, written and oral.

I emphasize building a solid mastery of knowledge. By revisiting past
accomplishments, I want to foster confidence and a spirit of independence. My
research space is built into an open lab environment, where mentees can observe
researchers at all levels in the midst of doing experiments. There are ample
opportunities to learn new methods and techniques, and also to witness the
challenges of conducting research. My door is open and the coffee machine is
within sight. I hope mentees drop by to talk about research. Once a week we
address the previous week's accomplishments, deal with unexpected issues, and
identify the set of goals for the next few weeks.

::: {.horizon-rule}
:::

## Teaching and mentoring education

**2022, The Inclusive STEM Teaching Project**  
Seven-week course engaging participants in reflection and discussion around
equity and inclusion in learning environments across a variety of institutional
contexts. Designed around identity, power, positionality, and privilege, with
the goal of improving participants' awareness, self-efficacy, and ability to
create inclusive STEM learning environments.

**2020, Active LENS Train-the-Trainers Workshop**  
Weeklong workshop on integrating the Avida-ED digital evolution learning
platform into coursework.

**2019, EPIC, University of Alaska Fairbanks**  
Two-semester, cohort-based program supporting UAF teachers developing and
delivering online courses.

**2016, Research Mentor Training, National Research Mentoring Network**  
Six-week synchronous online workshop focused on improving mentoring
relationships with undergraduate researchers, with a community of peers from
across the country.

**2015, iTeach, University of Alaska Fairbanks**  
Hands-on workshop from the Instructional Design Team at UAF eLearning and
Distance Education, covering research management, course scheduling, and
building and managing online learning communities.

**2007, Preparation for College Teaching, Washington State University**  
Formal instruction on strategies for teaching material in different contexts,
including student assessment beyond standard tests and quizzes, communication
skills for engaging students during lecture, and leadership and management
skills for combining an active research program with teaching responsibilities.
